'''Thomas Felix Rosenbaum''' (born February 20, 1955) is an American [[Condensed matter physics|condensed matter physicist]] and professor of [[physics]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech).<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=2018-07-30 |title=Thomas Felix Rosenbaum |url=https://labusinessjournal.com/news/thomas-felix-rosenbaum/ |access-date=2023-01-12 |website=Los Angeles Business Journal |language=en-US}}</ref> Prior to his time at Caltech, Rosenbaum served as a faculty member and [[Provost (education)|Provost]] of the [[University of Chicago]]. He has also served as the vice president for research at [[Argonne National Laboratory]].<ref>{{cite web |title=About President Rosenbaum |url=http://m.caltech.edu/content/about-president-rosenbaum |website=The California Institute of Technology |language=en |archive-date=2018-09-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180916123852/https://www.caltech.edu/content/about-president-rosenbaum }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=About President Rosenbaum |url=http://president.caltech.edu/about |access-date=2023-01-26 |website=Office of the President |language=en}}</ref>

Rosenbaum served as president of Caltech from 2014 to 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-07-01 |title=Caltech Welcomes Ray Jayawardhana as Tenth President |url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/caltech-welcomes-ray-jayawardhana-as-tenth-president |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=California Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref> His contributions ranged from boosting diversity in STEM through fellowships and research funding opportunities, to establishing a number of initiatives through the largest campaigns in Caltech's history.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Caltech Campaign Raises $3.4 Billion – Pasadena Now |url=https://www.pasadenanow.com/main/break-through-the-caltech-campaign-raises-3-4-billion-to-support-people-and-research-with-the-potential-to-change-the-world |access-date=2023-06-16 |website=www.pasadenanow.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Nietzel |first=Michael T. |title=CalTech's Capital Campaign Raises A Record $3.4 Billion |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaeltnietzel/2021/10/01/caltechs-capital-campaign-raises-a-record-34-billion/ |access-date=2023-06-16 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Rosenbaum grew up in [[Queens|Queens, New York City]], where he spent much of his time playing basketball and frequenting theater and jazz productions.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Episode 7 Transcript: A Formula for Success |url=http://thelonelyidea.caltech.edu/episode-7-thomas-rosenbaum-caltech-podcast |access-date=2023-06-16 |website=The Lonely Idea Podcast |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-12-10 |title=Q&A with Dr. Rosenbaum |url=https://magazine.caltech.edu/esblog/2014/12/10/qa-with-dr-rosenbaum |access-date=2023-06-16 |website=Caltech Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref> He is of German-Jewish descent, with both sets of his grandparents having left Germany after [[World War II]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://president.caltech.edu/speeches-and-writings/speech-transcripts/inaugural-address|title=Inaugural Address|website=Office of the President}}</ref> During the height of the [[Cold War]], Rosenbaum was inspired by the [[Apollo program]] and the [[Moon landing]]s to pursue physics as a means to solve the world's problems. He attended [[Forest Hills High School (New York)|Forest Hills High School]] in [[Queens]], and was a finalist in the 1973 [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]].<ref>{{cite news |title=New York Youths Win in Science |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1973/03/20/archives/4-new-york-youths-win-in-science-other-new-yorkers.html |work=The New York Times |date=March 20, 1973 |page=76}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Ajmera |first1=Maya |title=Conversations with Maya: Thomas Rosenbaum |url=https://www.sciencenews.org/sponsored/conversations-maya-thomas-rosenbaum |website=Science News |publisher=Society for Science & the Public |accessdate=28 April 2019}}</ref> He received his bachelor's degree in physics with honors from [[Harvard University]] in 1977. He then went on to work with Gordon A. Thomas at [[Princeton University]], where he earned his Ph.D. in 1982.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rosenbaum |first=Thomas F. |title=CURRICULUM VITAE |url=https://president.caltech.edu/documents/6733/tfrCV2020.pdf |access-date=25 June 2026 |website=[[Caltech]]}}</ref>{{Self-published inline|date=June 2026|certain=yes}}<ref name="thesis-rosenbaum-1982">{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/303077999 |title=Coulomb Interactions And Localization In A Disordered System |date=1982 |publisher=[[Princeton University]] |type=Ph.D. |last=Rosenbaum |first=Thomas F.|id={{ProQuest|303077999}} |url-access=subscription |oclc=79619652}}</ref>

== Career ==
Rosenbaum conducted research at [[Bell Laboratories]], Murray Hill, New Jersey, and at IBM [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center]], Yorktown Heights, New York, before he joined the [[University of Chicago]] faculty in 1983. From January 2007, Rosenbaum served as the provost of the University of Chicago. In addition to his responsibilities for academic and research programs across the university, Rosenbaum served and continues to serve on the board of governors for [[Argonne National Laboratory]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.uchicagoargonnellc.org/bios/rosenbaum.shtml|title=Thomas F. Rosenbaum|author=UChicago Argonne, LLC|date=|work=uchicagoargonnellc.org|accessdate=9 January 2016|archive-date=27 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180327084418/http://www.uchicagoargonnellc.org/bios/rosenbaum.shtml|url-status=dead}}</ref> He directed the university's Materials Research Laboratory from 1991 to 1994, the university's [[James Franck Institute]], an interdisciplinary research unit, from 1995 to 2001, and served as vice president for research and for Argonne National Laboratory from 2002 to 2006. He is a member of the board of directors of the ''[[Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists]]'' and the [[Santa Fe Institute]] Science Board, a trustee of the National Opinion Research Center (NORC), and a trustee of the University of Chicago Medical Center. Rosenbaum was announced as the eighth president of [[The California Institute of Technology]] on October 24, 2013 and took office at [[Caltech]] on or about July 1, 2014. Rosenbaum was formally inaugurated into the office on October 24, 2014.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-10-31 |title=The Inauguration of President Rosenbaum: A Recap |url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/inauguration-president-rosenbaum-recap-44344 |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=California Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref>

== Research ==
Rosenbaum is an expert on the [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanical]] nature of materials—the physics of electronic, magnetic, and optical materials at the atomic level—that are best observed at temperatures near absolute zero. Rosenbaum recognized early the significance and ubiquity of [[quantum phase transitions]]—from [[metal–insulator transition]]s<ref name="RosenbaumMilligan1983">{{cite journal|last1=Rosenbaum|first1=T.|last2=Milligan|first2=R.|last3=Paalanen|first3=M.|last4=Thomas|first4=G.|last5=Bhatt|first5=R.|last6=Lin|first6=W.|year=1983|title=Metal-insulator transition in a doped semiconductor|url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/47048/1/PhysRevB.27.7509.pdf|journal=Physical Review B|volume=27|issue=12|pages=7509–7523|bibcode=1983PhRvB..27.7509R|doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.27.7509|issn=0163-1829}}</ref> to [[magnetism]]<ref name="WuEllman1991">{{cite journal|last1=Wu|first1=Wenhao|last2=Ellman|first2=B.|last3=Rosenbaum|first3=T.|last4=Aeppli|first4=G.|last5=Reich|first5=D.|year=1991|title=From classical to quantum glass|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=67|issue=15|pages=2076–2079|bibcode=1991PhRvL..67.2076W|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.67.2076|issn=0031-9007|pmid=10044329}}</ref> to exotic [[superconductivity]]—and his work is recognized as putting quantum transitions on as solid a footing as that long available for classical transitions. He has both exploited and advanced methods in experimental low temperature physics, developing new techniques (hydrostatic pressure, stress, magnetometry, [[calorimetry]]) for high-resolution studies at milliKelvin temperatures, complementing laboratory dilution refrigerator approaches with synchrotron x-ray measurements in diamond anvil cells at [[cryogenic]] temperatures.<ref name="JaramilloFeng2009">{{cite journal|last1=Jaramillo|first1=R.|last2=Feng|first2=Yejun|last3=Lang|first3=J.C.|last4=Islam|first4=Z.|last5=Srajer|first5=G.|last6=Littlewood|first6=P. B.|last7=McWhan|first7=D. B.|last8=Rosenbaum|first8=T. F.|year=2009|title=Breakdown of the Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer ground state at a quantum phase transition|journal=Nature|volume=459|issue=7245|pages=405–409|bibcode=2009Natur.459..405J|doi=10.1038/nature08008|issn=0028-0836|pmid=19458718|s2cid=1692358}}</ref><ref name="FengWang2012">{{cite journal|last1=Feng|first1=Y.|last2=Wang|first2=J.|last3=Jaramillo|first3=R.|last4=van Wezel|first4=J.|last5=Haravifard|first5=S.|last6=Srajer|first6=G.|last7=Liu|first7=Y.|last8=Xu|first8=Z.- A.|last9=Littlewood|first9=P. B.|last10=Rosenbaum|first10=T. F.|year=2012|title=Order parameter fluctuations at a buried quantum critical point|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=109|issue=19|pages=7224–7229|arxiv=1109.0260|bibcode=2012PNAS..109.7224F|doi=10.1073/pnas.1202434109|issn=0027-8424|pmc=3358829|pmid=22529348|doi-access=free}}</ref> He established the nature of the metal-insulator transition in doped [[semiconductors]] and correlated materials,<ref name="HusmannYao1996">{{cite journal|last1=Husmann|first1=A.|last2=Yao|first2=X.|last3=Jin|first3=D. S.|last4=Zastavker|first4=Y. V.|last5=Rosenbaum|first5=T. F.|last6=Honig|first6=J. M.|year=1996|title=Dynamical Signature of the Mott-Hubbard Transition in Ni(S,Se)2|journal=Science|volume=274|issue=5294|pages=1874–1876|bibcode=1996Sci...274.1874H|doi=10.1126/science.274.5294.1874|issn=0036-8075|pmid=8943193|s2cid=45909959}}</ref> and demonstrated macroscopic anisotropy of non-s-wave superconductivity in [[heavy fermion]] compounds.<ref name="ShivaramJeong1986">{{cite journal|last1=Shivaram|first1=B.|last2=Jeong|first2=Y.|last3=Rosenbaum|first3=T.|last4=Hinks|first4=D.|year=1986|title=Anisotropy of Transverse Sound in the Heavy-Fermion Superconductor UPt_{3}|url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/47038/1/PhysRevLett.56.1078.pdf|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=56|issue=10|pages=1078–1081|bibcode=1986PhRvL..56.1078S|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.1078|issn=0031-9007|pmid=10032562}}</ref> Rosenbaum's experiments on magnets involve controllable tuning of quantum fluctuations in both ordered and disordered systems.<ref name="Brooke1999">{{cite journal|last1=Brooke|first1=J.|year=1999|title=Quantum Annealing of a Disordered Magnet|journal=Science|volume=284|issue=5415|pages=779–781|arxiv=cond-mat/0105238|bibcode=1999Sci...284..779B|doi=10.1126/science.284.5415.779|issn=0036-8075|pmid=10221904|s2cid=37564720}}</ref><ref name="BrookeRosenbaum2001">{{cite journal|last1=Brooke|first1=J.|last2=Rosenbaum|first2=T. F.|last3=Aeppli|first3=G.|year=2001|title=Tunable quantum tunnelling of magnetic domain walls|journal=Nature|volume=413|issue=6856|pages=610–613|arxiv=cond-mat/0202361|bibcode=2001Natur.413..610B|doi=10.1038/35098037|issn=0028-0836|pmid=11595942|s2cid=4404553}}</ref> He is interested in the macroscopic manifestations of [[quantum mechanics]]<ref name="GhoshRosenbaum2003">{{cite journal|last1=Ghosh|first1=S.|last2=Rosenbaum|first2=T. F.|last3=Aeppli|first3=G.|last4=Coppersmith|first4=S. N.|author4-link=Susan Coppersmith|year=2003|title=Entangled quantum state of magnetic dipoles|journal=Nature|volume=425|issue=6953|pages=48–51|arxiv=cond-mat/0402456|bibcode=2003Natur.425...48G|doi=10.1038/nature01888|issn=0028-0836|pmid=12955135|s2cid=4391669}}</ref> and harnessing disorder to craft a material's electrical, magnetic, and optical response.<ref name="SilevitchAeppli2010">{{cite journal|last1=Silevitch|first1=D. M.|last2=Aeppli|first2=G.|last3=Rosenbaum|first3=T. == Initiatives ==
[[File:Thomas Rosenbaum.jpg|thumb|Rosenbaum delivering an address at Caltech in 2017]]
During Rosenbaum's tenure as president of Caltech, the institute launched several new initiatives and research programs.<ref name=":0" /> Under Rosenbaum's leadership, Caltech launched the Resnick Sustainability Institute, the Bioscience Initiative, the Chen Neuroscience Institute, the Rothenberg Innovation Initiative, and the Merkin Translational Institute, among others.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-11-29 |title=How the $3.4 Billion Break Through Campaign Impacted Caltech |url=https://magazine.caltech.edu/post/break-through-campaign |access-date=2023-06-16 |website=Caltech Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref> More recently, Rosenbaum announced the Hurt Scholars Program and the Initiative for Caltech's Students, programs focused on student support and academic development.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-11-02 |title=New Professorships Support Early-Career Researchers |url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/new-professorships-support-early-career-researchers |access-date=2023-06-16 |website=California Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=About the Initiative - initiativeforstudents.caltech.edu |url=https://initiativeforstudents.caltech.edu/faq/ |access-date=2023-06-16 |website=initiativeforstudents.caltech.edu}}</ref> He also supported work in seismology at Caltech and advanced research initiatives at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL).<ref name=":0" />

Alongside his wife, [[Materials science|materials scientist]] [[Katherine Faber]], Rosenbaum has supported graduate fellowships and research funding opportunities. Among their most notable contributions is a fellowship they established at the University of Chicago's [[Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering at the University of Chicago|Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering]] in 2014.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-05-23 |title=Rosenbaum-Faber gift to support women in STEM fields through Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering {{!}} Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering {{!}} The University of Chicago |url=https://pme.uchicago.edu/news/rosenbaum-faber-gift-support-women-stem-fields-through-pritzker-school-molecular-engineering |access-date=2023-06-16 |website=pme.uchicago.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Rosenbaum and Faber also established the Guy Rindone Graduate Research Fund which supports graduate students in selecting research topics and broadening their educational experience.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Couple creates graduate research fund in honor of former Penn State professor {{!}} Penn State University |url=https://www.psu.edu/news/academics/story/couple-creates-graduate-research-fund-honor-former-penn-state-professor/ |access-date=2023-06-16 |website=www.psu.edu |language=en}}</ref> Their philanthropic work continued with their significant contribution to the [[Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation|Gordon and Betty Moore]] Graduate Fellowship Match at Caltech in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |title=home – initiativeforstudents.caltech.edu |url=https://initiativeforstudents.caltech.edu/ |access-date=2023-06-16 |website=initiativeforstudents.caltech.edu}}</ref> Following this, they initiated the Rosenbaum-Faber Family Graduate Fellowship. This fellowship underscores Rosenbaum's dedication to academic freedom, providing graduate students the flexibility to potentially adjust their research paths based on unforeseen results.

== Personal life ==
Rosenbaum is married to materials scientist and expert in [[ceramic engineering]] and [[Mechanics|mechanical behavior]], [[Katherine Faber|Katherine T. Faber]]. Together, they have two sons.

==Honors==
His honors include an [[Alfred P. Sloan Research Fellowship]], an NSF [[Presidential Young Investigator Award]], and the William McMillan Award for "outstanding contributions to condensed matter physics". Rosenbaum is an elected Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]], the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Thomas F. Rosenbaum {{!}} Office of the Provost |url=https://provost.uchicago.edu/directory/thomas-f-rosenbaum |access-date=2023-01-12 |website=provost.uchicago.edu}}</ref>
